title: Tools as altar vessels (Rule 31)
hook: the cellarer treats pots and tools like the vessels of the altar

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kitchen rota: a week each at serving, and nobody let off. Your line was everyone serves.

A dented saucepan. A spade with a split handle. A ladle left in the sink. Nobody would put them in a church. Yesterday the cooks handed the pots back to someone. Meet him. He's called the cellarer: the monk who keeps the stores, the food, the tools, the household goods. Benedict gives him a whole chapter, and in it one instruction turns the storeroom upside down. He is to look on every vessel and every possession of the monastery as if they were the sacred vessels of the altar. The chalice and the saucepan, handled with the same care.

Start with the man Benedict wants for the job: wise, steady, sober, not a big eater, not proud, not touchy, not slow, not wasteful, not stingy. Someone who'll be, the Rule says, like a father to the whole community. He looks after the sick, the children, guests and the poor. He lets nothing be neglected. And he treats the hoe and the bowl as if they belonged on the altar. Why would a pot be holy? One way to read it: in Benedict's house, there's no clean line where the sacred stops and the ordinary starts. The same God honored at the altar in the morning is served at the stove at noon. Carelessness with things is, in its small way, carelessness with the people who need them and the God who gave them. An old prophecy in Zechariah pictures this. On that day, even the bells on the horses carry the words holiness unto the Lord, and the temple pots are like the bowls before the altar. Then: "every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah shall be holiness unto the LORD of hosts." Every pot. The same chapter carries this care over to people. If a brother asks for something unreasonable, the cellarer mustn't sadden him with scorn. He should refuse humbly, and give a reason. And if he has nothing to give, he should at least give a kind word. A good word, the Rule says, borrowing from the book of Sirach, is above the best gift. A pot handled gently. A brother answered gently. The same care, pointed two ways.
screen: `A GOOD WORD ABOVE THE BEST GIFT.`

segments.voice: Pick up a tool that's near you, a mug, a pen, a knife, your phone, or picture one you use every day. Notice its weight, its scratches, the places your hand has worn, who made it and who it has fed or helped; later, clean it slowly, the way you'd handle something precious. If you pray, give thanks for it.
Tools as altar vessels. Benedict's word to his cellarer: treat every pot and tool as a sacred vessel of the altar.
Your line: every pot is holy. The saucepan too, handled like the chalice. Day one thousand one hundred eighteen.

howItsDone: In Benedictine houses the cellarer, or a monk or nun in that role, keeps the community's stores and goods, and the Rule's call to treat ordinary things as altar vessels shapes how the house's tools, kitchens and workshops are kept.

chat.says: Why would a monk treat a saucepan like something from the altar?
options: Benedict saw no clean line between sacred and ordinary; carelessness with things hurts the people they serve.
Because the Rule says the kitchen pots were also carried in and used at the altar on Sundays.
Because tools were scarce then, and Benedict cared mostly that nothing in the house got stolen.
chat.meaning: Benedict tells the cellarer to treat every vessel as the altar's sacred vessels. The same God honored at the altar is served at the stove.
